title: How Verstappen could prove tough to beat in Singapore Sprint
excerpt:
Max Verstappen came out on top in an intriguing Sprint Qualifying in Singapore, but while George Russell was an impressive second, his Mercedes team mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli – who is still running with the new-spec – was down in seventh.

Where did that Verstappen lap come from? Ferrari looked so good in SQ2...

Verstappen has proven time and time again over the years that he's capable of delivering the unexpected – and that was the case once again on Friday evening under the lights at Marina Bay as he stormed to a brilliant pole position in Sprint Qualifying.

title: Wolff fires back at ‘brainless’ driver treatment rumours
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has hit out at “completely nonsensical” suggestions that Mercedes have favoured Kimi Antonelli at times over George Russell, with the team boss stating that anybody who believes such rumours is “brainless”.

Antonelli currently leads the Drivers’ Championship by 84 points, a margin that grew last time out in Malaysia after Russell was forced to retire due to a power unit issue – marking the Briton’s third DNF of the season.

Speaking to the media on Friday at the Singapore Grand Prix, Wolff was quizzed on what he would say to those who feel that the Silver Arrows have favoured Antonelli amid speculation over the decisions that the team have taken regarding their drivers during the campaign.

“They're brainless,” the Team Principal responded. “Whoever thinks that… It's completely nonsensical. We've had it in the past with Lewis [Hamilton] fans. I don't know what's going on. Do they think I have a button, and that says ‘George engine failure now’? Or disadvantaging one driver against the other, when we're fighting for a Constructors’ Championship?

“We've always had the mindset of providing everybody with equal material, but I guess this is maybe where social media goes today. People hide behind their screens, and then they lash out. There's a lot of polarisation going on.”

Wolff went on to suggest that he could see the amusing side of such comments, adding: “Sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they're abusing the team or myself – I'm Satan, I've heard. So, yeah, overall, funny.

“But really zero understanding and respect for people who come up with these things. They should, rather than watching Formula 1, they should do Teletubbies or, I don't know, some Mickey Mouse.”

Wolff reiterated that he has long aimed for an equal and open approach when it comes to the drivers in the team.

“I've always tried, since I came into Formula 1, even in my Williams days, to be the most balanced and the most transparent with the drivers,” he explained.

“I remember being a complete rookie and running into Alain Prost on the grid of a race, and I said, ‘Just out of interest, why did it go so wrong between you and [Ayrton] Senna?’ And he said, ‘Because we never knew what the team was about.

Why splitting car specs is a 'no-brainer' for Mercedes

“’You felt that you were the flavour of the month at one time, and then two months later, you thought the politics were going against you. There were different situations where you had the feeling that you really were not wanted.’ So I took it as my challenge to keep it always balanced.

“It was not easy with Lewis and Nico [Rosberg] back in the day, and that's why, people can think what they want, but the integrity in that respect is something that's important for me, and the drivers know it.

“We have had Kimi since he was 11. He's an integral part of the team. It is very nice to see him grow, to be in a position now that he's fighting for a championship at such a young age, the talent he has.

“And then on the other side, George has been with us since he was 17. He’s someone I feel a lot of emotions for and compassion. We are very close. That's why it's pretty annoying to have some lunatics that have no understanding really about how relationships work coming up with these kinds of accusations.

“So I don't pay any attention to this. Most important is that George knows how the team is, and Kimi knows, and we will always try to give them equal opportunity.”

With Mercedes opting to split car specifications in Singapore – meaning that Antonelli is running the recent upgrade, while Russell has reverted back to his Azerbaijan-spec W17 – Wolff argued that this is an example of that equal approach.

“We don't know which one is going to be quicker, and so you take a decision to try to find out,” the Austrian said. “There is no great political thinking behind it. And when it comes to racing, like [McLaren’s] papaya rules, we have always been very clear that we're not standing in each other's way.

“We don't like the yo-yo racing that could cost the position if someone is close to us, and the quicker car, if it's behind, is always going to have an advantage, and that could go either direction. It doesn't matter. Even if it is now that it’s more realistic for Kimi to win a championship in sheer mathematical probability, we would still give George the same opportunities.

“And that's important. That's the ethos and the integrity on which the team has operated since 2013, since I came, and we wanted to stick to that, and then people can think what they want.”

title: Why Verstappen avoided a penalty after Sprint Qualifying
excerpt:
Max Verstappen put himself in the best spot for a Sprint victory at the Singapore Grand Prix after sealing pole in Sprint Qualifying.

However, the Dutchman initially faced some uncertainty over his position due to a potential yellow flag infringement during SQ1, an incident that was only investigated once the session was over.

Following the stewards’ hearing, it was confirmed that Verstappen would not receive a penalty – and we’ve rounded up the details on why that was the case.

What happened?

Single yellow flags were waved in SQ1 due to Cadillac’s Sergio Perez hitting the barriers, and Verstappen subsequently appeared to have overtaken the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton – prompting Hamilton to report over the radio: “Max overtook me under yellow flags.”

Verstappen then commented: “I’ll let Lewis by again. I think I passed him before the yellow, but I just want to be safe.”

A document released following the stewards’ hearing into the incident explains: “As Car 3 [Verstappen] was exiting Turn 7 on a push lap, a single yellow flag was displayed. Car 44 [Hamilton] was ahead of Car 3 and had been warned of Car 3’s approach.

“The driver of Car 44 said that after exiting Turn 7, he slowed and moved to the right to ensure he was off the racing line. Car 3 overtook Car 44 prior to Turn 8 while both cars were still in the yellow flag sector. Car 3 then abandoned the push lap.

“The driver of Car 3 explained that he was on throttle exiting Turn 7 and then saw the yellow flag and lifted. This was confirmed by telemetry. Within approximately 40 metres of entering the yellow flag sector, the driver of Car 3 had lifted fully off throttle. The driver of Car 44 was braking and had reduced speed to less than 60km/h at the point Car 3 overtook.”

Why didn’t Verstappen receive a penalty?

The stewards felt that Verstappen had “reacted appropriately to the yellow flag” and acknowledged that, while he had breached the regulation, this was “an unfortunate consequence of the significant closing speed differential”.

As the document states: “Because Car 3 was on a push lap and was on throttle out of Turn 7 and Car 44 had slowed, the speed differential at the point of the overlap was significant despite the fact that the driver of Car 3 had also started braking.

“The stewards were satisfied that the driver of Car 3 reacted appropriately to the yellow flag by lifting off throttle and reducing speed. The speed of Car 3 at the overtake point was some 70km/h less than Car 3’s speed on another push lap in the same session.

“The driver of Car 3 explained that to have avoided the overtake would have required him to have braked very heavily and he considered to have done so would have potentially created an unsafe situation.

“The stewards determined that the driver of Car 3 breached the yellow flag regulation by overtaking Car 44. However, the stewards were satisfied that the overtake was an unfortunate consequence of the significant closing speed differential and, in these circumstances, determined not to impose a penalty.”

This means that Verstappen retains his pole for Saturday’s Sprint at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, where he will line up ahead of Mercedes’ George Russell and Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc.

title: What the teams said – Sprint Qualifying in Singapore
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from Sprint Qualifying at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix.

Oct 09, 2026 4:52pm UTC

Red Bull

Neither Verstappen nor Hadjar ran the softs in FP1, leaving their true pace a little unknown going into Sprint Qualifying. Both drivers made it relatively comfortably into SQ3 but once there, Hadjar failed to set a time after running wide and losing his lap to track limits. Verstappen though nailed his final lap to grab pole by over a tenth, as he picked up where he left off in Sepang.

The Dutchman was called to the stewards to explain a moment in SQ1 where he seemed to overtake Hamilton under yellow flags, but they found no case to answer so Verstappen kept his pole position.

Max Verstappen, 1st, 1:31.156

“This was unexpected in Singapore, but I’m very happy to finish first today. We’ve been a lot stronger over the last few races, but this is a track that tends to highlight some of our weaknesses, and we had a few difficulties with the car early on. We managed to get the most out of it, and once we bolted on the Soft tyres the car really started to come alive. The extra grip gave us more confidence and stability in places where it had felt a bit uncertain before. Qualifying is the main goal tomorrow, along with making sure we get a good start. We’ll do our best and see what happens, but it’s been a positive way to start the weekend."

Isack Hadjar, 9th, No time set in SQ3

“We had a good start to the day with FP1, I felt comfortable straight away on the Hard compound and it was a positive session for us. Unfortunately, Sprint Qualifying wasn't so strong for me. I wasn't able to get a good lap in, and struggled with an issue on my last run. The Soft tyre felt like a big step compared to the Medium, I felt good on it but the car then became tricky to handle. We'll try and tweak the car a bit for tomorrow and make a step forward."

Hannah Schmitz, Head of Race Strategy

"It’s been a mixed day. SQ1 was quite disrupted, which meant we didn’t have a lot of data to work with heading into the next session. SQ2 went a bit more smoothly, and then in SQ3 it was great to secure Pole for the Team and Max. On the other side of the garage, we were managing an issue and Isack had his lap time deleted for track limits, which made it a more challenging day. The positive of a Sprint weekend is that there are still plenty of sessions ahead, giving us valuable opportunities to learn and prepare for Qualifying and the race, where the bigger points are on offer."

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Sprint Pole qualifier Max Verstappen of the Netherlands and Oracle Red Bull Racing looks on in parc ferme during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Isack Hadjar of France driving the (6) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

Mercedes

It was a mixed bag for Mercedes in Singapore, with some laps making them look the class of the field and others looking far more like they were struggling. Russell was back on the older spec package and it seemed to work well for him as he grabbed second on the grid for the Sprint. Antonelli remained running the latest Mercedes upgrades, although he did revert back to the old front wing after practice. But he could not find the same sort of pace as his team mate, winding up seventh – over half a second behind Russell.

Kimi Antonelli, 7th, 1:31.849

"It was a bit more of a tricky day for me today and it felt difficult to put a lap together unfortunately. From the first session onwards, I wasn't quite able to find the rhythm I was looking for and that made it hard to maximise the package when it mattered most. We still have more understanding to do in regard to our upgrade, and the focus will be on working through the data overnight to build a clearer picture of where we can improve.

"The positive is that we have plenty of information to look through and there are definitely areas where we can do a better job. The field is very close, so small changes can make a big difference. Hopefully we are able to find more performance and take a step forward tomorrow. I'll be giving it everything out on track and we'll see where that leaves us when it counts."

George Russell, 2nd, 1:31.276

"It's been a relatively good first day for me here in Singapore. We were competitive in FP1, topping the time sheets and my final lap in SQ3 felt good. We knew coming into the session that Max (Verstappen) was fast and unfortunately, we couldn't quite get ahead of him with that last effort. We can still be pleased with our efforts though. We got the car in a good place balance wise and that made it easier to extract the performance.

"We will now see what tomorrow brings in the Sprint. We saw that there's a big difference in grip from the left to the right side of the track here last year, with those lining up on the pole position side having an advantage. The task off the line tomorrow will likely be to maintain P2 and then see what we can do to challenge for victory from there."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"After a difficult weekend in Malaysia, we decided to run our cars in split specification this weekend here in Singapore. It is not the easiest track to do that at, or have the Sprint format, as it often takes a bit of time to get the car set-up dialled in. We've seen that today as whilst we're pleased to see George on the front row, it has left us with a bit of head scratching to do to understand why the update is not bringing the performance step we expect.

"Neither car had a great balance although Kimi was lacking more confidence on the braking and entry phase and that's what you need to attack a qualifying lap here. We'll keep working to understand why that's the case. We've got plenty of data around us to try and make some progress and hopefully we'll be able to get Kimi's car in a better place for main qualifying tomorrow."

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Sprint 2nd qualifier George Russell of Great Britain and Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team is interviewed during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Joe Portlock/Getty Images)

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Ferrari

Ferrari were in the mix from the word go, with both drivers looking quick at times. Hamilton has previous here with four poles at this track, but in the end it was Leclerc who proved the faster of the duo. He managed to grab a slot on the second row and crucially will start on the grippy side of the grid, while Hamilton was sixth after sliding his way around the track in the final sector.

Lewis Hamilton, 6th, 1:31.702

"In SQ3 we tried a different run plan, which in hindsight wasn’t the right call. The car felt good on the Mediums, but I struggled with rear grip on the Softs, especially on my final lap. We need to understand whether that came down to tyre preparation, balance or overheating. The pace was there earlier in the day and although it didn’t come together today, we’ll focus on what we’ve learnt and how to extract more tomorrow."

Charles Leclerc, 3rd, 1:31.399

"On my best lap, I got everything out of the car that we had today. There’s potential to improve for tomorrow with some fine tuning, so we can be there in the fight for pole. On a track like this, P3 is a good position to start the Sprint from, as overtaking will be difficult for all, so we will see what we can bring home."

Fred Vasseur, Team Principal

"As we expected, Sprint Qualifying was pretty closely fought. Our cars were better on the Medium tyres than with the Softs and we will work on improving our performance on this compound for tomorrow’s qualifying. Charles was competitive right to the end, while Lewis didn’t manage to put together an optimal lap in SQ3. We can expect a busy day tomorrow, with the Sprint race providing information that will be useful for Sunday and, after that, we will shift our focus to qualifying which takes place after the sun has set."

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Sprint 3rd qualifier Charles Leclerc of Monaco and Scuderia Ferrari is interviewed during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Joe Portlock/Getty Images)

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain and Scuderia Ferrari prepares to drive during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

McLaren

Norris has been struggling with a car issue, which McLaren believe is now fixed. It does seem to be better for the World Champion, who like his team mate was in the mix for the front rows. Once again, McLaren seem a fraction off the pace when it matters, with Piastri just 0.055s behind Leclerc. Norris was fifth, so the team could be on for double points tomorrow, but need to do some work to see if they can find anything extra ahead of Qualifying.

Lando Norris, 5th, 1:31.587

“P5 today, but not my best lap. Overall, the car is feeling good, and as a team, we are happy that things are working exactly as they should. However, the field is incredibly close, and you have to put in a perfect lap, which I unfortunately didn't manage to do. We'll review the data this evening, see what we can do from P5 on the grid tomorrow and then look to improve in tomorrow's Grand Prix Qualifying session.”

Oscar Piastri, 4th, 1:31.454

“P4. Overall, happy with that. I think we got close to the maximum of what we could have achieved today. It’s always difficult on a Sprint weekend to get everything right, but I was much happier than in the past few weeks with our performance. We were struggling quite a bit on the Mediums, but the car really came alive once we switched to the Softs. The added grip gave me the confidence to push, and it felt like a different car. That said, while the Soft was a big step in the right direction, it helped mask some issues so there's still work to do to find a more comfortable balance for the rest of the weekend. We’ll see what we can do in the Sprint tomorrow ahead of Grand Prix Qualifying.”

Andrea Stella, Team Principal

“It was an interesting Qualifying session, full of drama, which confirmed just how closely matched the frontrunners are. It’s no coincidence that there are four different cars in the top four positions.

“For our part, we’re reasonably satisfied with the result and the level of performance shown, as they’re a sign that, at least on this track, we’re back in a situation similar to that seen before Baku, when the differences in grid positions were relatively small. All things considered, it’s a good starting point for the rest of the weekend and we hope to be in contention for podiums.

“Certainly, some of our rivals have made progress in recent Grands Prix, in terms of performance, and today we saw further confirmation of that. We must continue to work on the car to optimise its potential as much as possible.

“As for how Sprint Qualifying went, there were some tricky moments in SQ1 because, in the final minutes, only a few cars, including ours, had set a meaningful time, but we managed to progress to the next round fairly comfortably. In SQ3, we decided to set two flying laps to allow the drivers to make the most of the switch from Medium to Soft tyres, particularly given that even the softer compounds are showing relatively limited degradation this year.

“Our attention now turns to the Sprint tomorrow evening, where we will continue to learn more about our car in these conditions, before preparing for Grand Prix Qualifying tomorrow night.”

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Lando Norris of Great Britain and McLaren prepares to drive during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Oscar Piastri of Australia driving the (81) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes in the Pitlane during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Anni Graf - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Racing Bulls

A very mixed session at Racing Bulls, with Lindblad out in SQ1 and Lawson making SQ3. The rookie struggled to find his rhythm at a new track after just the one practice session, and his case was not helped by disruption in SQ1 that limited his running. But Lawson put in a strong performance to start in the top eight, meaning if he can get off the line well, he could well fight for points and further extend his team’s advantage over Alpine in the standings.

Arvid Lindblad, 17th, 1:35.136

”It wasn’t the best Sprint Qualifying session. It’s a tough situation coming in as a rookie with only one Free Practice session at a street circuit, especially with the very different conditions under the lights compared to this afternoon. I wanted to complete a few laps in SQ1 to build up confidence, but the yellow flag meant we weren’t able to do that. I had a bit of a moment at Turn 13 and lost some time, which ultimately cost us a place in SQ2. All focus is now on to Qualifying tomorrow, where we’ll look to extract the maximum from the car and put ourselves in the best possible position for Sunday."

Liam Lawson, 8th, 1:32.341

"I feel pretty happy with today's Sprint Qualifying, particularly given we weren't strong during FP1. We made some changes in between sessions and they clearly paid off. It feels as though we're in a good place ahead of tomorrow and will of course push to stay within the points."

Dan Fallows, Technical Director

"We knew that the inaugural Sprint weekend in Singapore would present a challenge, particularly for Arvid, who has had just one practice session to get to grips with the circuit. Following a strong result for the team in Malaysia, we still had several setup items to try in FP1 as we looked to improve our competitiveness relative to Audi and Alpine. The heat and humidity also present challenges for brakes and cooling systems here, so we took the opportunity to make some tweaks to the car, which cost us some track time.

“Heading into Sprint Qualifying, we were conscious of the potential for disruption at a street circuit. Despite showing good pace, Arvid was unfortunate not to make it into SQ1. Liam made solid progress throughout the sessions however, building confidence in the car and delivering a fantastic lap to secure P8 on the grid for tomorrow’s Sprint.

“Some circuits this season have offered more overtaking opportunities than we initially expected, so we’ll be looking to see what opportunities present themselves tomorrow. The car has shown good pace here, and we’re hopeful of converting that into further Championship points across both the Sprint and Sunday’s race.”

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Liam Lawson of New Zealand and Visa Cash App Racing Bulls talks in the garage during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Arvid Lindblad of Great Britain driving the (41) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford on track during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Clive Rose/Getty Images)

Alpine

Alpine had a solid opening day in Singapore, looking right in the mix from the off. Gasly did make SQ3, his team mate just missing out thanks to a late improvement from Russell. In the final segment, Gasly’s lap time was deleted for track limits, leaving him P10, just ahead of Colapinto. Points might be tricky, but never say never, and the team should have enough data to try and move forward come Qualifying.

Pierre Gasly, 10th, No time set in SQ3

"The car has generally performed well today and we have looked competitive throughout the day. It was good to reach the top ten and be in SQ3. The pace and feel on the Mediums was good but, unfortunately, our run on the Softs was poor and I just felt like I had no grip. It was not a great feeling on that compound for some reason, so we have a bit of work to do in order to understand why that was the case. Obviously, the bigger picture is Sunday and that means Qualifying well tomorrow. So a bit of learning to do to see how we can extract the maximum tomorrow when we know it is even more important. Our focus in the meantime is to have a competitive Sprint and see if we can chase the top eight for points.”

Franco Colapinto, 11th, 1:33.249

“As always with Sprint weekends, you need to feel comfortable straight away in the car with limited practice time and we worked between the sessions to get it into a better place. SQ1 was a bit disrupted and stop and start, which stopped us getting into a rhythm and stringing a proper lap together, but we made it through. I struggled a bit at the start of the lap and think there's more performance to be found there. We put in a pretty good lap with the last run in SQ2, however it was not enough to progress, and a bit less than a tenth to Pierre and making it to SQ3. We know it will be tricky to overtake here and the start will be important, and from where we're starting we still have something to fight for. There's still some pace we can unlock from the car and hope to be in a stronger place for Qualifying also.”

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Sparks fly behind Pierre Gasly of France driving the (10) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: (EDITORS NOTE: Image has been digitally enhanced.) Franco Colapinto of Argentina driving the (43) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Pauline Ballet - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Audi

Audi’s day did not start brilliantly, with Hulkenberg pulling over in FP1 with a gearbox issue. The team managed to get that fixed in time for Sprint Qualifying, but it left the German short of laps. You would not have known that in SQ1, when he made it through into the next segment relatively comfortably, as did his team mate. But they could progress no further – Hulkenberg winding up two places ahead of Bortoleto despite being just 0.046s quicker.

Nico Hulkenberg, 12th, 1:33.420

"It was a decent Sprint Qualifying. We had a very strong run in SQ1, and while SQ2 wasn't quite as competitive, I think it reflected where we are at the moment. Considering we had limited running in FP1, I'm reasonably satisfied with how the session went.

"It's going to be a tough weekend: hot, humid and physically demanding. We'll take what we've learned today, see where we can make some improvements overnight and then focus on getting the most out of the Sprint tomorrow."

Gabriel Bortoleto, 14th, 1:33.466

“Everything was very close in SQ2. I feel my final lap was decent, but I left a little bit on the table in the last sector, with a big snap at the second-to-last corner. With such small gaps between cars, that makes a difference. Overall, it’s been an interesting day. We started well in FP1, but towards the end of practice we had a few issues, and I wasn’t as happy with the car. At the start of qualifying, we were also off the pace we expected, but we managed to make a step forward and I felt more confident as the session went on. Still, it wasn’t quite enough for SQ3. It’s still early in the weekend and we’re far from having everything optimised, so there’s plenty to work on.”

Allan McNish, Racing Director

“The first part of Sprint Qualifying is always a busy session for everybody, particularly with the red flag confining the crucial part to the final five minutes of action. We got through SQ1 reasonably comfortably and, while the first lap in SQ2 was good, the second wasn't quite optimal for either one of our drivers. Ultimately, Nico and Gabi were left in 12th and 14th respectively, with very little separating the two of them.

“I think we ultimately had the performance to be inside the top ten, and we were only a small margin away from achieving that. From a pure performance perspective, we have a clear focus for tomorrow's main qualifying session and will aim to make it one step further. However, before that we have the Sprint race, and we need to make sure we are in ready to make the most of any opportunity in that one, too.”

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Nico Hulkenberg of Germany driving the (27) Audi F1 Team R26 on track prior to practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Joe Portlock/Getty Images)

SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 09: Gabriel Bortoleto of Brazil driving the (5) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during Sprint Qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 09, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

Haas

Bearman was the pick of the two Haas drivers in Sprint Qualifying, but he was left a little confused at the end of SQ2. He initially believed he had driven a good enough lap to nearly make SQ3, but on hearing his position joked on the radio that he was “not that close.” As for Ocon, he'll start 16th thanks to a lock-up and might use the Sprint to gather valuable data to inform strategy for the Grand Prix.

Oliver Bearman, 13th, 1:33.423

“The car’s been feeling really good. We wanted to try something a little bit different, and based on what I felt so far in the car and the numbers, it didn’t seem to be ideal, but the feeling I had out there today was good. I felt a lot of confidence, and I could really push it, and that showed in the lap time as we were very close to SQ3. We had a very disrupted session in SQ2, with the first lap having to readjust from SQ1, where there were a few issues with the car. I think we can be happy with that result, and with a bit of fine-tuning, I think we can creep up there a little bit. Our target is the main race on Sunday and we’re close to the points there, so there’s every opportunity tomorrow afternoon to put ourselves in the best place.”

Esteban Ocon, 16th, 1:34.368

“We had a lock-up on the last lap that prevented us from a better qualifying. I was up quite a lot on the delta, so it’s a shame, but I've been having to push the car a lot this weekend. We’re on different specs to Ollie, so we’re just trying a few things which didn’t really work this session, and we changed a few parts on the car as well. We seem to have made a step backwards compared to FP1, where the feeling was good, so not a completely bad session – there are positives to take – but it’s not the way I wanted it to go in the end. It’s going to be tricky, but we take these learnings for the race, and the aim is to maximise qualifying tomorrow and start close to the top 10 on Sunday.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“It’s a Sprint weekend in Singapore, which is very exciting but hugely challenging as it’s a street circuit, and I think we did a good job in FP1. In SQ1, with the yellow and red flags, it was really challenging, but we did a good enough job to get out of SQ1. In SQ2, I think we left some performance out there. It was not to be for Williams, who lost both cars in SQ1. Sainz struggled and wound up at the back, with Albon not that much further forward. Whether they can improve come Qualifying remains to be seen, with those upgrades still not consistently pushing them up the order. “It wasn't the Sprint qualifying we wanted, and we need to understand why the car felt so different from FP1. There's work to do before tomorrow, and we'll see what we can learn in the Sprint to help set ourselves up for the rest of the weekend."

James Vowles, Team Principal

“A very frustrating evening. After the red flag in the first session of Sprint qualifying there was an issue with the way overtake mode was activated which definitely had an impact on our lap times. We are confident this will be fully investigated by the FIA.

“It was a pretty mixed up session with the Red Flag, and my second lap was a bit traffic-affected. It was quite a disrupted session so I couldn’t learn as much as I wanted to. I think we made some improvements from Practice and we’ll try to continue that direction for the rest of the weekend.”

Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal

“It was a tough Friday and Sprint Qualifying session for us in Singapore. Checo lost valuable track time in FP1 due to set-up changes in the garage, before experiencing some bottoming that caused him to hit a wall and damage his front wing during Sprint Qualifying. Valtteri's first timed lap was affected by yellow flags then was overtaken by another car while starting his last attempt at the end of the session, which affected his lap. Overall, a scrappy couple of sessions for us ahead of the Sprint tomorrow, and we will keep working on finding the best set up for our current package on this hot, dusty and challenging street circuit for Qualifying and the Race.”

Pirelli

Simone Berra, Pirelli Chief Engineer

"The level of track evolution was very significant from the very first session. If the circuit continues to improve at this rate, it is entirely possible that lap times tomorrow could be even quicker than initially forecast.

"From a tyre perspective, the factor that most differentiated the teams was warm-up. Others, however, were able to bring the tyres into the correct operating window very quickly, allowing them to push from the very first flying lap in qualifying.

"Today, teams focused more on single-lap performance than race pace because, with moderate temperatures and limited degradation, qualifying is likely to carry greater importance than race management. Between the C4 and C5 compounds, we measured a performance delta of around eight to nine tenths of a second, which is broadly in line with our expectations.

"One interesting aspect was the different approaches to qualifying lap preparation. Every team and driver adopted different strategies in terms of managing their attempts and cooling the tyres, while still extracting the best lap time available to them.

title: Stewards issue verdict over Verstappen yellow flag incident
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has avoided a grid penalty for Saturday’s Sprint in Singapore after being investigated for allegedly breaching yellow flag regulations during Sprint Qualifying.

Red Bull driver Verstappen was shown to have overtaken Ferrari rival Lewis Hamilton under yellows brought out when Sergio Perez’s Cadillac hit the barriers in the opening SQ1 phase.

“Max overtook me under yellow flags,” Hamilton promptly reported over the radio. Verstappen, meanwhile, commented: “I’ll let Lewis by again. I think I passed him before the yellow, but I just want to be safe.”

After noting the incident and then investigating it thoroughly post-session, the stewards determined that while Verstappen had indeed breached the yellow flag regulations, the circumstances around it meant his actions did not warrant a penalty.

The stewards’ decision document read: “As Car 3 [Verstappen] was exiting Turn 7 on a push lap, a single yellow flag was displayed. Car 44 [Hamilton] was ahead of Car 3 and had been warned of Car 3’s approach. The driver of Car 44 said that after exiting Turn 7, he slowed and moved to the right to ensure he was off the racing line. Car 3 overtook Car 44 prior to Turn 8 while both cars were still in the yellow flag sector. Car 3 then abandoned the push lap.

“The driver of Car 3 explained that he was on throttle exiting Turn 7 and then saw the yellow flag and lifted. This was confirmed by telemetry. Within approximately 40 metres of entering the yellow flag sector, the driver of Car 3 had lifted fully off throttle. The driver of Car 44 was braking and had reduced speed to less than 60km/h at the point Car 3 overtook.

“Because Car 3 was on a push lap and was on throttle out of Turn 7 and Car 44 had slowed, the speed differential at the point of the overlap was significant despite the fact that the driver of Car 3 had also started braking.

“The stewards were satisfied that the driver of Car 3 reacted appropriately to the yellow flag by lifting off throttle and reducing speed. The speed of Car 3 at the overtake point was some 70km/h less than Car 3’s speed on another push lap in the same session.

“The driver of Car 3 explained that to have avoided the overtake would have required him to have braked very heavily and he considered to have done so would have potentially created an unsafe situation.

“The stewards determined that the driver of Car 3 breached the yellow flag regulation by overtaking Car 44. However, the stewards were satisfied that the overtake was an unfortunate consequence of the significant closing speed differential and, in these circumstances, determined not to impose a penalty.”

Speaking before the stewards’ decision landed, an upbeat Verstappen – who claimed his and Red Bull’s first win of the season at Sepang last time out – explained how the RB22 “came alive a little bit more” through Sprint Qualifying.

He said: “It’s always close here in Singapore. Also your lap itself. You’re pushing as hard as you think is possible, close to the walls in places.

“For sure, once we bolted on the soft tyres [in SQ3], it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more, but I did not expect this. Of course, [I’m] very happy to be first.

“I think in the last few races we’ve been a lot stronger. This track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car, but we managed to drive with them as well as possible.”

title: McLaren pair divided over ‘very tricky’ Sprint Qualifying

title: Ferrari 'not fast enough' in Sprint Qualifying – Leclerc

"It was looking good in SQ1 and SQ2 and then I don't really know where it went away," he said.

title: Racing Bulls provide updated timeline as Liam Lawson awaits F1 future decision

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane has declared that it will finalise its 2027 driver line-up “in the coming weeks”.

The Red Bull sister team has enjoyed a positive season so far and is currently embroiled in a fight with Alpine for fifth in the constructors' championship.

title: Sergio Perez points 'aggressive' finger of blame for sprint qualifying crash

Sergio Perez has blamed a violent bottoming-out of his Cadillac for the crash that wrecked his lap during sprint qualifying at the Singapore Grand Prix.

title: Max Verstappen 'unsafe situation' sparks stewards verdict after Lewis Hamilton incident

Max Verstappen was investigated after sprint qualifying at the Singapore Grand Prix for a potential yellow-flag infringement.

Max Verstappen has escaped punishment from the stewards at the Singapore Grand Prix for a yellow-flag infringement in sprint qualifying.

It means Verstappen will start from pole position for the sprint at the Marina Bay Street Circuit on Saturday after beating George Russell and Charles Leclerc to the quickest effort under the lights in SQ3.

Midway through SQ1, however, a Sergio Perez crash triggered single yellow flags, starting the confluence of events that culminated with the Red Bull driver being investigated.

After his initial contact with the wall, the Cadillac driver left debris strewn across the track as he drove the ailing machine back to the pits.

That was eventually upgraded to a red flag, but beforehand, Verstappen was caught overtaking Lewis Hamilton directly underneath a yellow-flag light panel.

A large part of Perez's front wing was outside Verstappen on the edge of the corner, whilst the Ferrari had pulled over to the inside on the right, with the four-time F1 drivers' champion going past on the left.

According to the stewards' penalty guidelines, passing under single yellow-flag conditions in a qualifying session comes with a five-place grid penalty.

[Article continues below]

Explaining their decision not to punish Verstappen, a stewards' document read: "As car 3 [Verstappen] was exiting Turn 7 on a push lap, a single yellow flag was displayed. Car 44 [Hamilton] was ahead of car 3 and had been warned of car 3’s approach.

"The driver of car 44 said that after exiting Turn 7, he slowed and moved to the right to ensure he was off the racing line. Car 3 overtook car 44 prior to Turn 8 while both cars were still in the yellow flag sector. Car 3 then abandoned the push lap.

"The driver of car 3 explained that he was on throttle exiting Turn 7 and then saw the yellow flag and lifted. This was confirmed by telemetry. Within approximately 40 metres of entering the yellow flag sector, the driver of car 3 had lifted fully off throttle.

"The driver of car 44 was braking and had reduced speed to less than 60km/h at the point car 3 overtook. Because car 3 was on a push lap and was on throttle out of Turn 7 and car 44 had slowed, the speed differential at the point of the overlap was significant despite the fact that the driver of car 3 had also started braking.

"The stewards were satisfied that the driver of car 3 reacted appropriately to the yellow flag by lifting off the throttle and reducing speed.

"The speed of car 3 at the overtake point was some 70km/h less than car 3’s speed on another push lap in the same session.

"The driver of car 3 explained that to have avoided the overtake would have required him to have braked very heavily and he considered to have done so would have potentially created an unsafe situation.

"The stewards determined that the driver of car 3 breached the yellow flag regulation by overtaking car 44.

"However, the stewards were satisfied that the overtake was an unfortunate consequence of the significant closing speed differential and, in these circumstances, determined not to impose a penalty."

title: Red Bull issue 'virtually impossible' defence for Max Verstappen
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has mounted a strong defence of Max Verstappen after the four-time F1 champion was summoned to the stewards following sprint qualifying for the Singapore Grand Prix.

Verstappen topped SQ1, edging out George Russell and Charles Leclerc, but the session was overshadowed by an investigation into an overtake on Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton between Turns 7 and 8.

The yellow flags had been triggered after Sergio Perez crashed his Cadillac at Turn 5, scattering debris across the Marina Bay Street Circuit and ultimately bringing out a red flag.

Verstappen is understood to have told his team over the radio that he had passed Hamilton before entering the yellow-flag zone, and subsequently let the Ferrari driver back through to avoid a breach.

Speaking after the session, Mekies argued that the circumstances made the move unavoidable, pointing to the speed differential between the two cars.

"What I saw live was that Lewis was effectively on a cooldown lap, travelling at 50 kph or something, so it was virtually impossible for Max to stop by the time he saw the yellow and get onto Lewis at 50 kph," said Mekies, speaking to F1TV.

"He slowed down massively. I think he slowed down more than one second, which is huge for a single yellow.

"Realistically, he could not have been in a position to react fast enough to stop behind Lewis, let alone be safe."

Verstappen eventually went on to claim pole position for Saturday's sprint ahead of Mercedes' Russell and Leclerc in his Ferrari.

title: Carlos Sainz hits out at FIA over perceived lack of 'sporting equity'
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has voiced his dissatisfaction with the FIA over what he perceives to be a lack of "sporting equity" from motorsport's governing body.

Sainz implied bias was at play over some recent decisions taken, making reference to a call made last weekend at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

After the chaos on the formation lap at the Sepang International Circuit, the FIA opted to start the race in the original grid order, despite the regulations suggesting that the new, jumbled-up positions should have been used to determine who starts where once racing did eventually get underway.

Due to the disarray that took place on account of the "software bug" that plagued some cars, it was felt that common sense prevailed, with numerous cars displaced from their original positions and cars split across multiple laps.

Fast forward to sprint qualifying at the Singapore Grand Prix, an "unfortunate human error" during SQ1 meant that Overtake Mode was not activated once the session resumed following a Sergio Perez-induced red flag.

The FIA confirmed that it was subsequently turned on, but after just 27 seconds, it was actively disabled again, to try to preserve sporting fairness.

However, in doing so, this advantaged some drivers over others. Sainz, who qualified P22 and last under the lights at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, was not one of those, so was consequently disadvantaged — to the tune of half a second.

"Unfortunately, we had a really poor lap there," Sainz said after SQ1 in Singapore. "We only got one lap, and we had some issues with the brakes in FP1; we had to change them... [and] we were still having some brake issues — had a few lockups, struggling a lot with that and with the tyres."

Turning his attention to the issue at hand, which has since been confirmed to be the result of human error in race control, Sainz, who is also a Grand Prix Drivers' Association (GDPA) director, added: "But, on top of that, half of the cars did the lap with half a second quicker engine than the others.

"There was another software issue with the cars. This time around, we were on the bad end of it."

Sainz sees inconsistencies

Sainz was aggrieved by the FIA decision-making process seemingly advantaging bigger teams and drivers, with none of the headline names affected by the mistake in race control during SQ1.

"And for whatever reason, the FIA, like in Malaysia, didn't decide to do sporting equity, and were happy to do half of the cars in qualifying with a higher power than the other half of the cars," the four-time grand prix winner added.

"So a bit confused why the sport keeps doing different things depending on who is out in Q1 or who is out in Lap 1."

The Williams driver also stood to gain considerably after the disorder of the formation lap in Sepang, when the FIA decided to revert the grid order and nullify any changes in position.

At the time, Lewis Hamilton — who had qualified second alongside polesitter Max Verstappen — was the biggest name to be handed the reprieve, playing directly into Sainz's remarks.

title: Lewis Hamilton takes blame for crucial Singapore sprint qualifying mistake
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has taken the blame for an error during sprint qualifying, which he feels may have impacted his final result.

Hamilton ended the session in sixth place, marking a difficult result for him as he was outpaced by team-mate Charles Leclerc in third.

The seven-time champion was among a small handful of cars that opted to set an early lap during SQ3, rather than wait until the dying moments of the session when the track condition was at its peak.

It was a choice that Hamilton himself made, and suggested that it played a role in his lacklustre result.

“It was looking good in Q1 and Q2, and then I don't really know where it went away,” Hamilton said.

“We did a slightly different run plan to the others. It was my choice, and I think I got that wrong.”

Hamilton lacked tyre confidence in SQ3

However, he also acknowledged that the switch over to soft tyres for SQ3 brought its own challenges, having felt more comfortable on the mediums in the first two segments.

“But ultimately, just the car was very oversteery on that lap,” he said. “I don't know if the rears were not ready or if they're overheating.

“It was difficult to say, but it was very, very snappy, oversteery, and it just wasn't a good lap overall.

“On the mediums, it was good. Just much different on the softs, lots of grip, but only on the front and none at the rear.

“It could be balance, but ultimately I had the pace in the first two sessions, and then all of a sudden I didn't have the grip on the rear for some reason on that last lap.”

title: FIA reveal 'unfortunate human error' further influenced sprint qualifying
excerpt:
The FIA has reported that an "unfortunate human error" in race control meant Overtake Mode was unavailable after the red flag stoppage in SQ1 at the Singapore Grand Prix.

This issue was unrelated to the problems with F1's timing system during the first segment of sprint qualifying at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

However, it may have influenced the outcome of SQ1, with the motorsport governing body confirming that once the oversight was identified, Overtake Mode was reactivated for a period of 27 seconds before again being disabled.

The series of events occurred after the session was resumed following the Sergio Perez-induced red flag interruption.

"During the first period of Sprint Qualifying, there was a human error in Race Control unrelated to the timing issue also encountered in SQ1," the FIA said in a statement.

"This issue in question meant Overtake Mode was not available after the red flag period during SQ1. When it became apparent that Overtake Mode was not active after the restart, it was then activated for a period of 27 seconds before being deactivated again.

"The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap.

"The second and third periods of Sprint Qualifying were not affected."

It is not clear whether — or the extent to which — any cars were disadvantaged due to the problem, and which cars were able to access the added power that comes with Overtake Mode for those 27 seconds.

However, Carlos Sainz, who qualified last, has claimed he lost half a second. And Lawrence Stroll has claimed son Lance lost six tenths of a second.

The situation also explains why cars were not able to go faster than Lewis Hamilton's early benchmark time once the session resumed.

title: Max Verstappen voices Red Bull shock as Singapore sprint pole in doubt
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has admitted surprise over the performance of his Red Bull car during sprint qualifying after taking pole position for Saturday's race.

However, his result is under threat as he faces a stewards' investigation for allegedly overtaking under yellow flag conditions.

Verstappen entered the Singapore weekend on a high after taking his first race win of the year last time out in Sepang.

Continuing where he left off, Verstappen beat George Russell to the top of the timesheet by one-tenth of a second, marking the first time he has topped a sprint qualifying session this year.

“It's always close here in Singapore, and also your lap, you're pushing as hard as you think is possible, close to the walls in places,” he said.

“Once we bolted on the soft tyres, it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more.

“But I did not expect this, so of course, I'm very happy to be first.”

Verstappen will visit the stewards after moving in front of Lewis Hamilton during SQ1 through a yellow flag zone, which was deployed due to debris on the track.

However, with an investigation looming, Verstappen commended the work undertaken by Red Bull at recent events to improve its car.

“The last few races we have been a lot stronger,” he said.

“But of course, this track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car.

“But we managed to drive with them as well as possible.”

title: Max Verstappen stuns in sprint qualifying but pole under threat from investigation

Max Verstappen clinched pole position for the sprint at the Singapore Grand Prix, besting George Russell by just over a tenth of a second under the lights of the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Charles Leclerc rounded out the top three, ahead of the McLarens of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris.

Verstappen overcame an ERS issue before the sprint qualifying, with Red Bull making precautionary changes to his RB22.
